items.stem: In Spark, which of these is an action that triggers execution of the built-up plan?

options.rationale: Correct: count() is an action that forces the DAG to execute.
filter() is a lazy transformation; it adds to the plan.
select() is a transformation and does not trigger execution.
withColumn() is a transformation, evaluated lazily.

items.explanation: Correct: count() is an action that forces the DAG to execute.

items.stem: You join a very large fact table to a small lookup table. Which strategy usually avoids an expensive shuffle?

options.text: Broadcast the small table to every executor
options.rationale: Correct: broadcasting the small side lets each executor join locally without shuffling the large table.

options.text: Repartition the large table by a random key
options.rationale: A random repartition adds a shuffle rather than avoiding one.

options.text: Collect both tables to the driver
options.rationale: Collecting large data to the driver risks running out of memory.
Caching does not remove the shuffle a hash join needs.

items.explanation: Correct: broadcasting the small side lets each executor join locally without shuffling the large table.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about Spark DataFrame operations are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Transformations are lazy and build a plan until an action runs
options.rationale: Correct: Spark defers transformations until an action forces execution.

options.text: Built-in functions generally outperform equivalent Python UDFs
options.rationale: Correct: built-ins run in the JVM and avoid per-row Python serialization.

options.text: Every transformation immediately reads all data from disk
Caching always speeds up a job regardless of reuse
options.rationale: Caching helps only when data is reused; otherwise it wastes memory.

items.explanation: Correct: Spark defers transformations until an action forces execution.; Correct: built-ins run in the JVM and avoid per-row Python serialization.
